definition: Ineffable means impossible to express in words.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ineffable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ineffable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The perfumer can name three hundred scents on a strip, but the smell of the sea before a storm defeats her — ineffable, she says, and stops trying.
A moving performance stirs real feeling that you can happily describe all the way home; ineffable experience is different in kind — the feeling is vivid, and the telling is impossible.
An overwhelming feeling floods you, yet the words for it usually arrive by morning; ineffable is the far shore — no words arrive at all.

Inexpressible is ineffable's everyday twin: the feeling cannot be put into words. Ineffable says the same thing in a hush, with a shade of grandeur — writers keep it for awe, grief, and joy at their outermost edges, where inexpressible would do the job but without the candlelight.

Unspeakable also says words fail, but English has assigned it to the dark: unspeakable cruelty, unspeakable loss. Ineffable faces the light — wonder, gratitude, joy past phrasing. The two words refuse language for opposite kinds of experience, one from horror and one from awe.

The linguist had four working languages and a career built on precise definitions, yet at her daughter's citizenship swearing-in she found herself with nothing to say: not tearful exactly, not proud exactly — some braid of relief, grief for the old country, and hope that had no name in any of her dictionaries.
That is ineffable: not hard to phrase, but past phrasing.
Ineffable is the honest surrender: in- (not) + effari (to speak out) — what cannot be spoken out.
It differs from private, which is unshared by choice, and from vague, which is unclear even to you.
The ineffable feeling is vivid and entirely yours; only the bridge into words is out.
Ineffable admits defeat grandly: the experience is vivid, and words are not invited.

If words could manage it with effort, say hard to describe; if you'd simply rather not share, that's private, not ineffable.

The science writer had prepared for the eclipse the way she prepared for everything: interviews with astronomers, a glossary of terms, two pages of notes on what the corona would look like.
Then totality arrived, the light went strange and silver, and the birds stopped singing.
Her editor found her afterward staring at a blank page.
The word she finally filed was ineffable, and she spent the rest of the column admitting it was the only honest one.
Readers wrote in agreeing.
The strangest letters came from engineers, who apologized for their sentences and sent diagrams instead.
Every fact she had gathered survived the afternoon, she wrote; it was the feeling that no sentence would hold.
